assignments.title: 🌌 Beyond the Light: Life on the Space Station
assignments.html:
🌌 Beyond the Light: Life on the Space Station

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.1 – Recognize that there are enormous distances between objects in space and apply knowledge of the speed of light and light travel time to understand these distances.

🎯 Objective

Independently write a science-based narrative from the perspective of a child living on a space station, explaining how scientists use light, light-years, and light travel time to understand the vast distances in space.

Students will demonstrate understanding through accurate science explanations, clear reasoning, and a supporting AI-generated visual.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Imagine growing up in space.

From your window aboard a space station, Earth is a glowing blue sphere below you. Stars shine brighter than you’ve ever seen before. Some of that light began its journey millions or even billions of years ago—long before you were born.

Living in space has taught you something important: space is unimaginably vast, and scientists cannot measure it the same way we measure distances on Earth.

Your mission is to tell the story of what you have learned about distance in space, and how light helps humans understand the universe. 🌠

🧰 Step 1: Writing Task

You will write a short piece from the perspective of a child living on a space station.

Your writing should explain:

  • Why space distances are hard to understand

  • How scientists use the speed of light

  • What a light-year really measures

  • Why looking into space is like looking back in time

  • Why space travel is extremely difficult

Your story should blend personal experience with accurate science explanations.

📝 Step 2: Writing Requirements

  • At least 3 paragraphs

  • Each paragraph must be 4–6 complete sentences

  • Written in first person (I, me, my)

  • Clear cause-and-effect explanations

  • Accurate, on-topic science

👉 Before submitting, double-check that you have used and underlined at least 5 vocabulary words.

🧪 Step 3: Required Science Concepts

Your writing must include all of the following:

🌟 Speed of Light

  • About 300,000 km per second

  • Light is extremely fast, but still takes time to travel

🌠 Light-Years

  • A unit of distance, not time

  • Used to measure distances between stars and galaxies

🕰️ Light Travel Time

  • We see objects as they were in the past

  • Distance determines how far back in time we are seeing

🚀 Space Travel vs. Light

  • Spacecraft travel much slower than light

  • Traveling to stars would take thousands of years

📚 Vocabulary

Correctly use at least 5 of the following terms in your writing and underline each vocabulary word when it appears.

  • Light-year

  • Speed of light

  • Distance

  • Space travel

  • Light travel time

  • Universe

👉 Reminder: Vocabulary words only count if they are underlined and used correctly.

✍️ Step 4: Writing Format Options

Choose ONE submission format:

📝 Option 1: Handwritten (Science Notebook)

  • Write neatly in your science notebook

  • Take a clear, well-lit photo

  • Writing and underlines must be easy to read

📸 Blurry or unreadable photos will be returned for resubmission.

💻 Option 2: Typed

  • Type your writing in a Word document or Google Doc

  • Use proper paragraph formatting

  • Underline vocabulary words

  • Attach the file to the assignment

🎨 Step 5: Design a Visual Using AI

Create an AI-generated visual that represents your life on the space station and what you’ve learned about distance in space.

Your image must include:

  • A space station, astronaut viewpoint, or scene from your story

  • Stars, galaxies, or light traveling through space

  • A title that matches your writing

🧠 AI Prompt Example (You MUST Create Your Own)

Your AI prompt could look something like this, but it must match your story.

Your AI prompt should match your story and may be in any art style (cartoon, anime, realistic, illustrated, etc.). Remember to be specific. Describe your story and what you chose to write.

Example Prompt:

“A detailed illustration from the perspective of a child looking out a space station window at distant stars and galaxies. Beams of light stretch across space showing light-years and the vast scale of the universe. The scene feels quiet, reflective, and educational.”

📝 Step 6: Assignment Submission

Submit ALL of the following:

📄 1. Written Piece
A complete narrative written from the perspective of a child on a space station, including at least 5 underlined vocabulary words.

🖼️ 2. AI-Generated Visual

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 10 Correct explanation of light-years, speed of light, and space distance aligned to SC.8.E.5.1
📚 Vocabulary Use 5 Uses at least 5 vocabulary terms, correctly and underlined
✍️ Perspective & Explanation 10 Strong first-person perspective as a child on a space station with clear, accurate explanations
🎨 AI Visual 5 Image clearly supports the writing and science concepts

💯 This assignment is worth 30 points total.

assignments.title: 🌌 Beyond the Stars: A VR Tour of the Universe
assignments.html:
🌌 Beyond the Stars: A VR Tour of the Universe

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.2 – Describe the characteristics of the universe, including stars, galaxies, and the scale of the universe.

🎯 Objective

Independently create a VR video report explaining the structure of the universe and Earth’s place within it.

Students will demonstrate understanding of galaxies, stars, gravity, and the immense scale of the universe through accurate science explanations, correct vocabulary usage, and verbal communication in VR.

🌌 Mission Briefing

The universe is vast — far larger than anything we experience on Earth.

It contains hundreds of billions to trillions of galaxies, and each galaxy contains billions of stars. Our home, Earth, exists on a single planet orbiting one star inside one galaxy — the Milky Way.

Even though space may appear empty, it is filled with stars, galaxies, gas, dust, and energy. Gravity holds these massive systems together, shaping the structure of the universe on an unimaginable scale.

Your mission is to step into virtual reality as a cosmic guide and explain what the universe is made of, how galaxies and stars fit into it, and how Earth fits into the bigger picture.

Your goal is to help someone understand scale — showing how small Earth is compared to the universe, and why that matters scientifically. 🌠

🧰 Step 1: Focus of Your VR Report

Your VR video report will focus on galaxies, stars, and the scale of the universe.

In your report, you will explain:

  • How galaxies are organized within the universe

  • How stars exist within galaxies

  • How Earth fits into this larger structure

Your goal is to help someone understand how large the universe is and where Earth belongs within it.

This is not a list of facts — it is an explanation of scale, relationships, and structure in space.

🎥 Step 2: VR Video Report Requirements

Record a 60–90 second VR video report explaining the structure and scale of the universe.

Your video should clearly walk through each step below. This is a spoken scientific explanation, not a script you read.

1️⃣ Explain what the universe is

Clearly explain what scientists mean by the universe.

Include:

  • What the universe contains

  • That it includes all space, matter, and energy

  • That everything that exists is part of the universe

2️⃣ Describe what a galaxy is

Explain what a galaxy is and why galaxies are important.

Include:

  • What galaxies are made of

  • That galaxies contain billions of stars

  • That galaxies are held together by gravity

You may mention different galaxy shapes (spiral, elliptical, irregular) if helpful.

3️⃣ Explain the role of stars in galaxies

Describe what a star is and how stars fit into galaxies.

Include:

  • That stars are massive, glowing balls of hot gas

  • That stars produce light and energy

  • That galaxies contain stars of different sizes and temperatures

Be sure to explain that our Sun is one star among many.

4️⃣ Explain the scale of the universe

This is the most important part of your report.

Explain:

  • That the universe contains billions to trillions of galaxies

  • That each galaxy contains billions of stars

  • Why these numbers are difficult for humans to imagine

Use scale language such as:

  • enormous, vast, unimaginably large, far beyond Earth

5️⃣ Explain Earth’s place in the universe

Clearly explain where Earth fits.

Include:

  • Earth → Solar System → Milky Way → Universe

  • That Earth is not the center

  • That our location is one of many

Connect this to why understanding scale matters.

📚 Step 3: Required Vocabulary

Correctly use at least 5 vocabulary words from the list below during your VR video report.

Core Vocabulary

  • Universe

  • Galaxy

  • Star

  • Milky Way

  • Gravity

  • Scale

  • Solar system

👉 Vocabulary only counts if it is used correctly and in context during your explanation.

⭐ Bonus Opportunity: Constellation Precision (+2 points)

Students may earn up to 2 bonus points by including a specific constellation in their VR video report.

To earn bonus points:

  • Name a real constellation

  • Draw the constellation accurately on the VR blackboard

  • Ensure the star pattern matches the real constellation shape

  • Briefly explain how constellations help humans organize and understand the night sky

Artistic style does not matter — accuracy does.

➡️ This bonus is optional and will not affect your base score.

🧠 Important Reminder

Your presentation style may vary, but the science expectations do not.

Every report must clearly show that:

  • The universe contains galaxies and stars

  • Galaxies are held together by gravity

  • Earth is a very small part of a much larger universe

  • Understanding scale helps explain our place in space

🎮 Step 4: VR Environment

Choose a VR environment that helps you explain the universe.

You may:

  • Point to stars or galaxies

  • Gesture to show size and distance

  • Use the blackboard to sketch or label ideas

The environment does not need to be exact — your scientific explanation matters most.

📝 Step 5: Assignment Submission

Submit ALL of the following:

🎥 1. VR Video Report (2D Video Only)
A clear, complete explanation that meets all science and vocabulary requirements.

⚠️ Important Reminder:
Your submission must be a 2D video recording, not a spatial recording.

💡 Quick Tip (Read Before Submitting)

If you accidentally record a spatial recording and need to resubmit:

  • Load your spatial recording

  • Play it back

  • Then take a 2D video of your recording while it plays

This allows you to submit the correct format without re-recording your entire presentation.

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 10 Correct explanation of galaxies, stars, and the scale of the universe
📚 Vocabulary Use 5 At least 5 terms used correctly
🎤 Clarity & Explanation 10 Clear, organized explanation of scale and structure
🎮 VR Engagement 5 On-task use of VR to support explanation
Total 30 points

⭐ Bonus: Up to +2 points for an accurate constellation drawn and explained on the VR blackboard.

💯 This assignment is worth 30 points total, with up to 2 bonus points available.

assignments.html:
📰 OPTIMA Times: The Cosmic Hierarchy Special Issue

Breaking News: Earth’s Address in the Universe Revealed!

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.3– Recognize that the universe contains many billions of galaxies and that each galaxy contains many billions of stars.

🎯 Objective

Use AI tools and Canva to design a science magazine cover for The OPTIMA Times that explains the hierarchy of the universe — showing how objects in space are organized from smallest to largest.

Your mission: report on the structure of the universe like a science journalist, using visuals and headlines to explain how Earth fits into a much larger cosmic system.

💬 Essential Question

“How is the universe organized, and where does Earth fit within that structure?”

🧠 Mission Briefing

Breaking news from deep space, Science Correspondent! 🌌

The universe may seem endless and chaotic, but scientists have discovered that space is organized in a clear hierarchy. Smaller objects belong to larger systems, and each level is part of something even bigger.

From the planet beneath your feet to the farthest galaxies ever observed, everything in space fits into a layered structure:

  • Planets belong to solar systems

  • Solar systems belong to galaxies

  • Galaxies belong to the universe

Understanding this hierarchy helps scientists explain scale, distance, and Earth’s place in the cosmos.

Your assignment is to investigate one level of the universal hierarchy and report on how it fits into the larger structure for a special issue of The OPTIMA Times.

You are both the scientist and the journalist — translating big-picture space science into something the public can understand.

🧩 Assignment Steps

1️⃣ Choose Your Level of the Universe

Select ONE level of the cosmic hierarchy to feature on your magazine cover:

🌍 Planet
☀️ Solar System
🌌 Galaxy
🌠 Universe

Your focus should explain:

  • What your level is

  • What it contains

  • How it fits into the level above it

2️⃣ Generate Your Visual

Use an AI image generator to create a clear, accurate visual that represents your chosen level of the universe.

Your image must:

  • Clearly show the scale of your level

  • Be scientifically accurate

  • Look appropriate for a science magazine

  • Leave space for headlines and text

This image will be the main cover photo for your magazine.

3️⃣ Design Your Magazine Cover in Canva

Go to Canva and search for magazine cover template.

Choose a layout that fits a science, space, or news magazine.

Your cover must include:

  • 📰 Magazine Title: OPTIMA Times

  • 🗞️ Main Headline related to your chosen level of the universe

  • 📝 A supporting headline and blurbs

  • 🖼️ Your AI-generated image

Your final product should look like a real magazine cover, not a poster or slideshow.
Take a look at my example Magazine cover about Volcanos!!

4️⃣ Science Content Requirements

Your magazine cover text must clearly explain:

  • What your level of the universe is

  • What objects it contains

  • How it fits into the larger hierarchy

  • Why understanding this level helps scientists understand the universe

An OPTIMA Science Comic Special Issue

📜 Standard:

SC.8.E.5.3 – Compare and contrast the properties of objects in the solar system and beyond including distance, size, and composition.

🎯 Objective

Independently create a hand-drawn science comic that explains how objects in space are organized and distinguishedby:

  • 📏 Distance

Students will demonstrate understanding of hierarchy in space through accurate science explanations, correct vocabulary usage, and clear visual storytelling.

🌌 Mission Briefing

At first glance, space looks like chaos.

Stars scattered everywhere.
Planets drifting in the dark.
Galaxies floating like islands in an endless ocean.

But space is not random.

It is organized.

Everything in the universe belongs to a system of order — a hierarchy — where objects are arranged by size, distance, and what they are made of.

Moons orbit planets.
Planets orbit stars.
Stars belong to solar systems.
Solar systems belong to galaxies.

And at every level, the scale changes dramatically.

Some objects are small and rocky.
Some are enormous and made of gas.
Some are so far away that their distances are measured in light-years.

Scientists do not classify space objects using just one property.

They use multiple clues:

  • How big something is

  • How far away it is

  • What it is made of

Your mission is to tell the story of how the universe is organized — and how scientists use distance, size, and composition to put everything in its proper place.

You will tell this story through the eyes of an astronaut traveling outward through space, discovering how the universe is organized step by step.

Your goal is to explain the system, not just name objects — showing that the universe is not just big, but ordered and understandable. 🌌

🧰 Step 1: Your Story Frame

  • 🌕 Moons

  • 🪐 Planets

  • ☀️ Stars

  • 🌌 A solar system

  • 🌠 A galaxy

  • How distance increases

  • How size changes

  • How what objects are made of (composition) is different at each level

  • Galaxies are separated by millions of light-years

You must show that:

Distance increases dramatically at each level of the hierarchy.

📐 Size Differences

Your comic must show that:

  • Moons < Planets

  • Planets < Stars

  • Solar systems < Galaxies

You must also show that:

  • A galaxy contains billions of stars

  • Size increases as you move up the hierarchy

🥼 Demonstration Station: Gravity & Motion in Space

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.4– Explain that gravity is the force that not only keeps planets in orbit around the Sun, but also controls the formation of stars, planets, and solar systems.

🎯 Objective
Independently create a demonstration scene that shows how gravity controls motion in space.

Through this task, students will model how gravity affects orbits, paths of motion, and speed at different scales in the universe. Students will demonstrate understanding by building, labeling, and explaining gravitational interactions using visual models and in-world sticky notes rather than written paragraphs.

This assignment is designed to help students move beyond identifying gravity as a force and instead focus on how gravity and motion work together to create predictable patterns such as orbits. By the end of this activity, students should be able to show that gravity controls motion from moons and planets to stars and galaxies.

🌌 Mission Briefing
Gravity does not just form objects in space — it controls how they move.

Objects in space are always moving forward, but gravity pulls them inward.
The balance between forward motion and gravitational pull creates curved paths called orbits.

Gravity determines:

  • The path an object follows

  • How fast it moves

  • Whether a system stays stable or falls apart

Because gravity follows consistent rules, motion in space is predictable.

Scientists use this predictability to:

  • Track planets

  • Predict eclipses

  • Navigate spacecraft

Your mission is to step into virtual reality as a space systems scientist and enter the Demonstration Station.

You will build, label, and explain how gravity controls motion using visual models and in-world sticky notes.

Your goal is not just to name gravity’s effects, but to prove how gravity and motion work together to create stable, predictable systems in space. 🪐

🧰 Step 1: Choose a Gravity & Motion Interaction to Demonstrate
Choose ONE gravitational interaction to demonstrate, or combine multiple for a more advanced model.

🌍 Planetary Orbits

Planets move around stars because of gravity.

Examples you can model:

  • A planet orbiting a star

  • A curved orbital path

  • Planets closer to a star moving faster

  • Planets farther away moving slower

Key ideas:

  • Gravity pulls inward

  • Forward motion keeps the planet from falling straight in

  • Distance affects orbital speed

🌕 Moons & Planetary Gravity

Moons orbit planets due to gravitational pull.

Examples you can model:

  • A moon orbiting a planet

  • Curved paths around the planet

  • Predictable orbital motion

Key ideas:

  • Planets have gravity

  • Gravity controls the moon’s path and speed

🔄 Gravity & Motion Balance

Orbits exist because of a balance between forces.

Examples you can model:

  • Forward motion vs. inward pull

  • What happens if gravity is stronger or weaker

  • How changing speed affects the orbit

Key ideas:

  • Too little speed → collision

  • Too much speed → escape

  • Balanced motion → orbit

🌌 Large-Scale Motion (Advanced Examples)

Gravity works on every scale of the universe.

Examples:

  • Stars orbiting within a galaxy

  • Galaxies moving within clusters

  • Gravity holding large systems together

Key ideas:

  • Gravity acts over huge distances

  • Larger mass = stronger gravitational pull

🎮 Step 2: Demonstration Scene Requirements
Build a scene that clearly shows how gravity controls motion.

Your demonstration must include ALL of the following:

    • Explain the motion being shown

  • Distance affects orbital speed

  • Motion in space follows predictable patterns

🌌 Classifying & Comparing Stars

Part 1 – Stellar Evolution & Mass

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.5 – Describe and classify specific physical properties of stars: apparent magnitude (brightness), temperature (color), size, and luminosity.

🎯 Objective

In Part 1 of this two-week project, you will model how stars form, live, and die.

You will examine how a star’s mass determines:

  • Its size

  • Its temperature

  • Its luminosity

  • Its lifespan

  • Its final stage

Stars are not all the same. Some live for billions of years. Others burn hot and fast, ending in massive explosions.

Your task is to build a visual model that compares the life cycles of a low-mass star and a high-mass star, and explain how mass determines destiny.

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

  • Describe the stages of stellar evolution

  • Compare low-mass and high-mass stars

  • Explain why mass determines lifespan

  • Describe how energy production changes over time

  • Predict the final stage of a star based on its mass

This week focuses on stellar evolution and energy changes before we organize stars on an H–R diagram next week.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Stars begin in massive clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.

Gravity pulls material together.
Pressure increases.
Temperature rises.


When nuclear fusion begins in the core, a star is born.

But not all stars follow the same path.

⭐ Low-mass stars:

  • Burn fuel slowly

  • Live longer

  • Become red giants

  • End as white dwarfs

🔥 High-mass stars:

  • Burn fuel quickly

  • Shine brighter

  • Become red supergiants

  • End in supernova explosions

  • May form neutron stars or black holes

The key difference is mass.

Mass determines:

  • Core pressure

  • Fusion rate

  • Temperature

  • Luminosity

  • Lifespan

Your mission is to model these two evolutionary paths and explain the role of mass in shaping a star’s life.

You are building a comparison model of stellar evolution.

🔥 A High-Mass Star Life Cycle

  • Protostar

  • Main Sequence Star

  • Red Giant (low mass) OR Red Supergiant (high mass)

  • Final stage (White Dwarf OR Supernova → Neutron Star / Black Hole)

  • Increasing pressure and temperature

  • Beginning of collapse

  • Hydrogen as the main material

🌟 Protostar

  • Collapsing sphere of gas

  • Increasing brightness

Explain:

  • Core temperature rising

  • Energy from gravitational collapse

  • Fusion has NOT started yet

  • Star is not yet stable

🌞 Main Sequence Star

Include:

  • Stable star

  • Balanced size and brightness

Explain:

  • Hydrogen fusion in the core

  • Energy released as light and heat

  • Balance between gravity (inward) and pressure (outward)

  • The Sun is currently a main sequence star

🔴 Red Giant (Low-Mass Star)

  • Expanded outer layers

  • Larger size

  • Cooler surface

Explain:

  • Hydrogen in the core running out

  • Core contracts

  • Outer layers expand

  • Fusion moves to outer layers

🔴 Red Supergiant (High-Mass Star)

  • Extreme expansion

  • Very high luminosity

Explain:

  • Fusion of heavier elements

  • High core temperature

  • Short lifespan

  • Rapid fuel use

💥 Final Stages

🌟 Low-Mass Star → White Dwarf

Include:

  • Small, dense core

  • No fusion

Explain:

  • Outer layers shed

  • Core remains and slowly cools

  • Explosion

  • Ejected outer layers

Explain:

  • Fusion stops at iron

  • Neutron Star (very dense remnant)

🎯 Objective
In this investigation, you will build a SunSlice model — a 3D physical model of the Sun that shows its internal layers and solar activity.

Scientists study the Sun by examining its structure, energy movement, and surface activity. Because the Sun is too large and too hot to visit directly, scientists build models to help visualize how our star works.

• The structure of the Sun

☀️ Mission Briefing

The Sun is a massive sphere of hot plasma that produces enormous amounts of energy through nuclear fusion in its core.

Scientists study the Sun by observing its internal structure and dynamic surface activity.

The Sun contains several major layers:

• Core – where nuclear fusion produces energy
• Radiative Zone – energy slowly moves outward through radiation
• Convective Zone – hot plasma rises while cooler plasma sinks, transferring energy through convection
• Photosphere – the visible surface of the Sun

The Sun is also extremely active.

Astronomers observe features such as:

• Sunspots – cooler, darker regions on the photosphere
• Solar flares – sudden bursts of energy released from magnetic activity
• Prominences – giant loops of glowing plasma extending outward from the Sun

The Sun is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System. Its powerful gravity controls the motion of planets and influences how they move through space.

Earth follows the same rules as the other planets, but it has conditions that make it unique. Earth also has a natural satellite — the Moon, which orbits Earth due to gravity.

From our recent study of stars, we also know that the Sun is classified as a medium-sized main sequence star. Main sequence stars produce energy through nuclear fusion and make up most of the stars in the universe.

The constellations we see in the night sky are patterns formed by distant stars, reminding us that the Sun is just one star among billions in our galaxy.

🧠 Putting AI to the Test: Solar System Models

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.8 – Compare various historical models of the Solar System, including geocentric and heliocentric systems.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will use an AI image generator to create a scientific diagram comparing historical models of the solar system.

Throughout history, humans have tried to understand how the solar system works. Early observers noticed patterns in the sky, such as the daily movement of the Sun, Moon, and stars. Based on these observations, scientists developed models to explain how objects in space move.

A scientific model is a representation used to explain how a system works. Models can include diagrams, drawings, physical models, or mathematical explanations. Scientists use models when something is too large, too small, or too complex to observe directly.

One of the earliest models was the geocentric model, which placed Earth at the center of the universe. According to this model, the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars revolved around Earth.

Later, scientists developed the heliocentric model, which placed the Sun at the center of the solar system. In this model, Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun. Earth also rotates on its axis, explaining the daily motion of the Sun across the sky.

As new evidence and better technology became available, scientists realized the heliocentric model explained planetary motion much more accurately than the geocentric model.

In this assignment, you will put AI to the test by generating a visual model of the solar system and evaluating how accurately the AI represents the historical models.

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Identify the geocentric and heliocentric models
• Compare how the two models explain planetary motion
• Explain why the heliocentric model replaced the geocentric model
• Evaluate whether an AI-generated diagram accurately represents scientific models

🌌 Mission Briefing

Scientific knowledge changes over time as new evidence becomes available.

Early scientists used the observations they had to create models explaining how the solar system worked. As technology improved, scientists collected new evidence that led them to revise these models.

The transition from the geocentric model to the heliocentric model is one of the most important examples of how scientific understanding evolves.

Your mission is to use AI as a scientific tool to generate a visual model of the solar system and then analyze how well the AI represents the historical models.

🧰 Your Task

You will use an AI image generator to create a scientific diagram comparing the geocentric and heliocentric models.

You may use any AI image generator, including:

• Canva Magic Media
• ChatGPT image generator
• Grok
• Another AI tool of your choice

Your generated image should clearly show how the two models represent the solar system.

After generating the image, you will add labels and write a scientific explanation comparing the models.

Step 1 — Identify the Two Models

Your diagram must include both:

• The Geocentric Model (Earth-centered system)
• The Heliocentric Model (Sun-centered system)

Your image should clearly show:

• Which object is at the center of each model
• How planets move in each model
• The position of Earth relative to the Sun

Step 2 — Write Your AI Prompt

Before generating your image, write a clear prompt describing the scientific diagram you want the AI to create.

Your prompt should include:

• Both solar system models
• Labels for Earth and the Sun
• Planetary orbits
• An educational science diagram style

Example prompt:

“Educational science diagram comparing the geocentric and heliocentric models of the solar system, Earth at the center in one model and the Sun at the center in the other, planets orbiting, labeled scientific illustration.”

Generate 2–3 images and choose the one that best represents the science.

⚠️ Important: The example prompt above is only provided to show how prompts work.
You may NOT copy or use my prompt for your image.

You must create your own prompt using your own wording.

AI tools often generate very similar images when the same prompt is used, which makes it easy to identify copied prompts. If the same prompt is used, the images will look nearly identical and it will be clear that the example prompt was used.

Your goal is to construct your own prompt like a scientist giving instructions to a computer model.

Step 3 — Add Scientific Labels

Download your image and add at least five science labels.

Examples of labels include:

• Geocentric Model

• Earth
• Sun
• Planetary Orbit
• Retrograde Motion

Your diagram should clearly show the difference between the two models.

You may add labels using Canva, Google Slides, PowerPoint, or another drawing tool.

Step 4 — Explain the Models

Write 4–6 sentences explaining:

• What the geocentric model shows
• What the heliocentric model shows
• One reason scientists eventually replaced the geocentric model
• How new evidence helped scientists improve the model

Your explanation should show that scientific models can change as new evidence becomes available.

Be sure to spell check your writing and use proper grammar, capitalization, and punctuation before submitting.

🧠 Reflection Writing

Scientists evaluate tools and models to determine how accurately they represent scientific ideas.

Write a 4–6 sentence reflection explaining:

An OPTIMA Science Comic Special Issue

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.11 – “Describe how energy from space is received on Earth by electromagnetic waves, which can be used to study the universe.”

🎯 Objective
Independently create a science comic that explains how electromagnetic waves travel through space and how scientists use them to study Earth and the universe.

Students will demonstrate understanding of how energy from space is transferred through electromagnetic waves by modeling wavelength, frequency, and energy relationships, as well as how different types of waves are used in scientific observations.

Through this assignment, students will explain how electromagnetic waves vary across the spectrum and how these differences allow scientists to gather information about objects that cannot be observed using visible light alone.

By the end of this assignment, students should be able to visually and scientifically explain how electromagnetic waves are used to study space, Earth systems, and real-world phenomena.

🌌 Mission Briefing
Energy from space is constantly reaching Earth.

But much of this energy cannot be seen.

This energy travels as electromagnetic waves—waves that move through empty space carrying information from distant objects such as the Sun, stars, and galaxies.

These waves vary in wavelength, frequency, and energy.

Some waves are long and carry low energy.
Others are short and carry extremely high energy.

Together, these waves form the electromagnetic spectrum.

While visible light allows us to see, it represents only a small portion of the spectrum.

Other types of waves—such as infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays—reveal information that cannot be seen with the human eye.

Scientists use these waves to study temperature, composition, motion, and energy in space.

Satellites and scientific instruments collect this data and allow us to observe patterns, detect changes, and better understand the universe.

Your mission is to take this complex system and turn it into a clear, visual explanation.

You are not just creating a comic—you are modeling how electromagnetic waves are used to explore and understand the world beyond what we can see.

⚠️ Comic Focus: Read Carefully

This comic is a little different than the other comic editions we have created this year.

In this assignment, your focus is not just on storytelling—it is on the science behind how electromagnetic waves are used.

You are using the comic book / graphic novel format as a tool to explain relationships and real-world applications step-by-step.

Each panel should build on the previous one and clearly show how electromagnetic waves vary and how scientists use them to gather information.

You are not just drawing a comic—you are modeling how science is used to understand the universe.

🛰️ The Edge of Exploration: Designing Technology for the Unknown

📜 Standard:
SC.8.E.5.10 – Describe how technology is used to access, gather, store, and analyze information related to Earth’s systems and space exploration.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will design and build an original piece of technology in VR that allows scientists to explore a remote part of the solar system.

Scientists rely on technology to study environments that are too far, too dangerous, or impossible for humans to reach. These environments include distant planets, moons, and deep space regions.

Technology allows scientists to:
• Collect data
• Take accurate measurements
• Explore extreme environments
• Communicate discoveries

In this assignment, you will act as a scientist and engineer, creating a new invention that helps scientists explore the cosmos.

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Explain why technology is necessary for space exploration
• Describe how technology helps scientists study remote locations
• Design a solution to a real scientific challenge
• Communicate how your invention functions and collects data

🌌 Mission Briefing

The lights dim and your screen flickers to life as a distorted signal cuts through the silence.

“…this is Station Helios… do you copy…”

The transmission breaks in and out, but one thing is clear—scientists have lost contact with their deep space probes.

Coordinates flash across your display: Europa, Titan, Neptune, the Kuiper Belt.

A second voice comes through, more urgent this time.

Extreme temperatures, rising radiation levels, and unknown environmental conditions are causing current technology to fail. Rovers are shutting down. Satellites are losing signal. Probes are no longer transmitting data.

For decades, scientists have relied on technology to explore the solar system. But now, the environments they are trying to study are more extreme than ever before.

Some regions are so cold that materials freeze instantly. Others are filled with radiation that destroys electronics. Some are so far away that communication takes hours—or even days.

Scientists cannot travel to these locations themselves. They must rely on technology to extend human reach beyond physical limits.

Without new technology:
• Data cannot be collected
• Samples cannot be gathered
• Discoveries cannot be made

The future of space exploration depends on innovation.

You have been selected as part of the Next Generation Exploration Team—a group of scientists and engineers tasked with solving this problem.

Your mission is to design a piece of technology that can survive extreme environments, operate in a remote location, collect meaningful scientific data, and send that data back to Earth.

Every design decision you make must solve a real scientific challenge.

The signal flickers one last time.

“…we are counting on you…”

Your screen clears. The build environment loads.

🧪 Lab Environment

➡️ Enter a Science Lab environment in ENGAGE VR

➡️ Build your model on a lab workstation or table

Your build should feel like:
• A scaled planetary surface model
• A controlled engineering test environment
• A scientific prototype setup, not a full environment

💡 Mission Reminder
The greatest discoveries in science happen because someone builds the technology to reach the unknown.

Now it’s your turn. 🚀

🧰 Your Task

You will design and build a tabletop planetary exploration model in VR.

Your model will include:
• A scaled surface environment (planet, moon, or space region)
• A custom-designed piece of technology that operates within that environment

Your build should stay contained to a lab workstation/table-sized space.

Think of your model as something scientists would use to test and explain their technology. A scientist should be able to look at your lab and clearly understand:
• Where the technology is operating
• What problem it is solving
• How it functions in that environment

They should be able to predict how your technology will perform before it even begins operating.

🌍 Step 1— Choose Your Environment

You must choose ONE location your technology will explore:

• A planet (Mars, Neptune, etc.)
• A moon (Europa, Titan, etc.)
• An asteroid or comet
• Deep space beyond our solar system

🌌 Step 2— Build the Surface

On your lab table, you will:

• Create a scaled version of the surface
• Include key environmental features (ice, rock, terrain, atmosphere, etc.)
• Represent environmental challenges (extreme cold, radiation, pressure, uneven terrain, etc.)

Your surface should clearly show what makes this location difficult to explore.

🤖 Step 3— Design Your Technology

Your invention MUST include:

• A clear purpose (What is it designed to do?)
• A way to survive the environment (temperature, radiation, pressure, etc.)
• A way to move or operate (wheels, flying, drilling, floating, etc.)
• A way to collect data or samples
• A way to send information back to Earth

Your technology must be clearly placed and interacting with your surface model.

🛠️ Step 4— Build Your Model in VR

Inside VR, you will:

• Build your surface on a lab table or workstation
• Add your invention to that environment
• Use the 3D Pen, IFX objects, and other VR tools
• Create a clear, connected structure (not floating or random parts)
• Show how your invention works through its design

Your model should clearly represent a real scientific solution.

🧾 Step 5— Sticky Note Explanations

You MUST use sticky notes in VR to explain your invention.

Your sticky notes must clearly show how your technology is used to study space, not just what it looks like.

Your sticky notes must include:

• The name of your invention
• The location it is exploring (planet, moon, etc.)
• What problem it solves

🔬 Technology & Data

• How your technology collects data
(What is it measuring—images, temperature, radiation, samples, etc.?)

• How your technology gathers or accesses information
(How does it reach or interact with the environment?)

• How your technology stores data
(Where is the information kept?)

• How your technology sends or communicates data back to Earth

• How scientists use the data
(What can be learned and why it matters)

🛠️ Structure & Function

• Labeled parts of your invention
• What each part does
• How the parts work together

Your sticky notes should allow someone to fully understand how your technology works without you explaining it out loud.

If a scientist cannot understand how your technology collects and uses data, it is not fully complete.

🧠 Step 6— Scientific Thinking

Your invention must show that you understand:

• Why scientists need technology to explore space
• The challenges of remote environments
• How tools collect and send data

This is not just a build. It is a scientific solution.

🌎 Required Components

✔ Tabletop planetary surface model
✔ Original exploration technology
✔ Clear interaction between technology and environment
✔ Sticky note explanations

📸 Submission Requirement— Pictures

To submit this assignment, you must upload pictures of your VR build.

Your submission must include:

Your pictures must clearly show both your design AND your explanations.
